board.title: Spain Housing General Strike

header.title: Spain Housing General Strike
header.subtitle: Nationwide general strike and housing protests across Spanish cities

headline.text: Following Spain's November 11 general strike over the housing crisis, at least 115 people have been arrested and snap national elections are set for November 29.

sentences.text: Unions and housing groups held a 24-hour general strike on November 11—Spain's first in 14 years—to demand lower housing costs and higher wages after Parliament rejected two housing bills.

Assessments of participation conflict sharply: unions called the stoppage massive and estimated four million demonstrators nationwide, while employers called it a failure with workplace turnout under 5%.

The strike halted industrial plants, blocked major roads, cancelled over 280 flights and 111 long-distance trains, and severely disrupted public transit, though storms forced rally cancellations in Cádiz, Huelva, Córdoba, and Sevilla.
Evening marches drew tens of thousands in Barcelona and 120,000 in Madrid, ending in clashes with police that left 20 protesters injured; arrest counts ranged from 74 to at least 115 nationwide.
Unions have announced legal complaints over the police operations, while Spain prepares for snap general elections triggered by the housing crisis and strike on November 29.

sources.title: Millions of Spaniards stage first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing | CNN
sources.snippet:
Four million Spanish workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, unions said, enduring stormy weather to set up picket lines in a protest against the country’s housing affordability crisis less than three weeks before a snap general election.
Spain’s fast-growing hospitality and finance industries are less unionised than the public and industrial sectors. Police had reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents linked to the general strike, including blockades of offices and industrial estates and burning of rubbish containers. Unions said they would file a criminal complaint against what they described as a “disproportionate” response during a police operation involving tear gas and batons that left 20 protesters injured. The strike follows weeks of demonstrations provoked by the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid. Those protests, along with parliament’s rejection last month of government decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting rent pressures, prompted Sanchez to call the snap election. The strike was seen as a success by unions, with high participation reported in sectors like automotive and ports, although business owners' groups claimed it had limited impact. The strike's slogan, "Salaries. Housing. Prices," reflects the deep frustration over housing costs, which have become a central issue in the upcoming election. Housing activists and unions are demanding government intervention to curb real estate speculation and provide more protections for renters. --- Sponsored Content Sponsored Content
